sentences.text: Episode 15 ended on a picture we never explained. Two hundred providers on the funnel, and a quarter of them outside it.
When the providers were identical, about one in twenty fell outside. That was luck, and we knew how much of it to expect.
A quarter is something else. Luck does not stretch that far.
So is a quarter of the crowd outliers? Or is something wrong with the test?
Neither. The test is answering a question that has stopped being useful.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today, the last episode: wider than chance.
Our crowd has a knob: how much providers truly differ. Set it to zero, and every ordinary provider is the same.
Give each one its z: its distance from the reference, in units of what luck allows. The pile of them hugs the bell curve, and 11 of the 194 are flagged.
Now turn the knob, in three steps.
The pile spreads. And the flags climb: 16, then 35, then 48.
At the last setting, a typical provider's odds differ from the reference by roughly 30%. That is not much. But it is real, and the test can see it.
Look at who is flagged. Of the providers with 200 patients or more, 40%. Of those with fewer than 50, 7%.
The reason fits in one line. A provider's z spreads by chance, and also by its true distance from the reference, measured against how precisely we know it.
For a provider known to within 0.1, that second part swamps the first. Its z has three times the spread that chance alone would give, and it is flagged more than half the time.
Large providers are not worse. They are measured better, so their small true differences show.
So nothing is wrong with the test. Every one of those flags is true: that provider is not exactly at the reference.
But with enough patients, nobody is. The question has stopped sorting providers.
Here is a better one. Not: is this provider exactly at the reference? But: is this provider unusual, among providers?
To answer that, we stop taking the bell curve on faith, and fit one to the providers themselves: to the central bulk of their z-values.
That fitted curve is called an empirical null.
We do it separately for small, medium and large providers. The fitted spreads are 1.14, 1.60 and 2.18.
Judge each provider against its own group's curve, and 13 are flagged, in place of 52.
Across twenty redraws of the crowd, the share of ordinary providers flagged falls from 23% to 5%.
On the funnel, it is a wider pair of limits for each size group. For a provider of 280 patients, they move from 0.76 and 1.24 out to 0.50 and 1.57.
It is not free. Of our six planted providers, the standard test caught four. This one catches three.
The curve is itself an estimate, and it can miss. With the knob back at zero, this crowd's curves came out too narrow, and flagged 20 where the standard test flagged 11.
And it assumes that most providers are ordinary. If many are not, the curve widens to hide them.
Above all, it has not made anything more exact. It has changed the question. A flag now means: unusual among providers.
There are other answers too: the shrunken estimates of Episode 17, or no flags at all, only intervals.
Let's gather it up.
When providers truly differ a little, their test statistics spread wider than chance, most of all for large providers.
The standard test asks whether a provider is exactly at the reference. The empirical null asks whether it is unusual among providers.
Choosing between them is choosing what a flag should mean.
And that is the logistic fixed-effect model, from an unfair comparison to a flag you can defend.

One intercept for every provider. A fit that balances observed against expected. A ratio that asks what the reference would have done with the same patients. And a test that knows how far luck can reach.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
